extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science and philosophy (scientists, philosophers, advanced students of epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming, interpreting, and evaluating scientific laws and for distinguishing scientific/descriptive notions of law from civil/moral and metaphysical usages. Emphasizes criteria for what counts as a good scientific law, proper inference, and limits of explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish three senses of 'law'
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep distinct the perceptive order, the descriptive order, and the prescriptive order (i.e., the routine of sense-impressions, the brief description or formula of science, and the canon of social conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate civil/moral law, the mere concatenation of phenomena, and scientific formulae; strive to use separate terms for each sense of 'law' and ensure the sense intended is clear on each occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific law as a brief descriptive formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific laws are 'brief statements or formulae which describe [the] sequences and relationships' of phenomena; they 'economize thought' by giving simple, short descriptions of wide sequences of sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good scientific law is simple and concise while covering a wide range of phenomena; examples: Kepler's laws vs Newton's law of gravitation (Newton's is briefer, more accurate, and more wide-embracing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and simplicity criterion for fundamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider the range of phenomena embraced, and the simpler the statement of the law, the more nearly it is a 'fundamental law of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or formulating laws, prefer formulations that increase coverage and reduce complexity, provided they remain empirically adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testability as the final test
rubrics_metrics.description: The only final test of the truth or sufficiency of any law is the actual comparison of the results of the formula with the facts themselves — historical observation or physical experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish hypothesis from law by subjecting claims to observation/experiment; every law must return to hypothesis with increased perceptive powers and be retested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisionality and replacability of scientific laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific laws are always liable to be replaced by wider generalizations; earlier formulae are not necessarily wrong but may be insufficient and superseded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat laws as provisional best-descriptions not final metaphysical truths; be open to reformulation as new data or broader syntheses arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newton's canon (parsimony of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not seek superfluous causes for natural phenomena; 'We ought not to look for new causes to explain any group of phenomena until we have shown that no known cause is capable of explaining it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid positing unnecessary entities or unknown 'reasons' (anti-pattern: invoking metaphysical or extraneous agents before exhausting known explanations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid projecting human reason into nature (argument from design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious of inferring that reason (or a lawgiver) exists behind phenomena merely because scientific formulae exhibit order; the 'reason' we find in natural phenomena is put there by human reason when we classify and formulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not commit the fallacy of moving from pattern in descriptions to assuming an external rational agent; distinguish the product of human classification from any metaphysical claim about the universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate concatenation of phenomena from scientific law
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the mere concatenation or routine of sense-impressions (natural law in older sense) from the mental formula (scientific law) which gives brief expression to their sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid confusing observed sequences themselves with the conceptual description of those sequences; recognize that the scientist's formula is a mental shorthand, not the phenomena themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject appeals to supersensuous/metaphysical entities without necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicist's 'supersensuous' conceptions (atoms, molecules) are intellectual tools potentially lacking direct sense-impressions; the metaphysician's supersensuous posits an existence unconditioned by perception — the latter is an unproven dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanations that remain within or tied to perceptual/experimental basis; do not conflate useful ideal concepts with claims about unconditioned realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality is conditional on human faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality or apparent absoluteness of scientific law is relative to the human mind and conditioned by (1) the perceptive faculty and (2) the reflective faculty; laws assume similarity across normal human beings' faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming universality, account for variability in perceptive/reflective faculties (e.g., different species or disordered minds perceive differently); universality is practical, not metaphysical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for selectivity of perceptive faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceptive faculty is a selective 'sorting-machine' that determines which sense-impressions form 'reality' for a being; different organisms perceive different realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that empirical data and the resulting laws depend on which sensations are selected by the perceiver; include consideration of observer limitations and selection effects when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat routine of perceptions as possibly endogenous
rubrics_metrics.description: Before appealing to the unknowable or supersensuous, the scientific tendency is to consider the routine of our perceptions as due in some way to the structure of our perceptive faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer parsimonious, testable accounts that attribute perceptual routines to known faculties/causes rather than to inscrutable or metaphysical sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil/moral law vs scientific law: do not conflate
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil law originates in custom and is laid down by intelligent beings for others; natural (scientific) law is not a command and is valid for all normal human beings — civil law is a natural product but not identical with scientific law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing 'law' claims, clarify whether the discourse is prescriptive (civil/moral) or descriptive (scientific); failure to separate leads to fallacies (examples: Stoics equating civil law with natural law).
